title: gio/outputstream: increase splice buffer size
description:
Usually when using splice you're trying to copy a potentially large
amount of data. 256kb tends to be the "right size" for this sort of
thing empirically, famously for things like `cat`.

In our case, it also can save considerable GTask/threadpool overhead
under some situations depending on the VFS backends being used since
you effectively reduce some syscall overhead by 32x.
author: chergert

title: tiles: Preserve pointer offset during custom tile resize
description: Interactive resizing of a custom tile currently snaps its selected boundary directly to the pointer when the resize starts, which is especially disruptive when several tiled windows share that boundary. This change uses pointer deltas to preserve the initial pointer-to-boundary offset, selects a corner from the pointer quadrant, and resolves horizontal and vertical edges independently. If a requested edge touches the output boundary, the opposite available inner edge is used. Existing Quick Tile behavior is unchanged. Tested with kwin-testTiles, kwin-testMoveResize, and manually in a Plasma Wayland session with a three-window custom tile layout.

title: alsa-card-profiles: add profile set for the Audeze Maxwell
description:
## What this adds

A profile set and three mixer paths for the Audeze Maxwell, plus udev entries for three product IDs:

| ID | Device | Verified |
|----|--------|----------|
| `3329:4b18` | Maxwell XBOX Dongle | On hardware, numbers below |
| `3329:4b1e` | Maxwell XBOX Headset, own USB cable | On hardware, numbers below |
| `3329:4b19` | Maxwell Dongle, the non-XBOX variant | Not held. Inferred from the reporter's logs in #4513 |

Closes #4513. Nothing outside the new files changes except three lines in `90-pipewire-alsa.rules`.

`4b19` is the only line I cannot vouch for from hardware, and it is the one the issue reporter has. If you would rather not take it on inference, drop that line and the `Closes` with it, since the remaining two IDs do not cover their device. Details in the last section.

## Why usb-gaming-headset.conf does not work here

The dongle splits playback into a chat stream and a game stream, so that profile set looks like the right one, and #4513 is someone forcing it with a udev rule and finding both volume sliders move together.

`usb-gaming-headset-output-stereo.conf` ends with a hardcoded element index:

```
[Element PCM,1]
```

Both output mappings in `usb-gaming-headset.conf` reference that path:

```
[Mapping stereo-chat]
device-strings = hw:%f,0,0
paths-output = usb-gaming-headset-output-stereo

[Mapping stereo-game]
device-strings = hw:%f,1,0
paths-output = usb-gaming-headset-output-stereo
```

On a headset whose only playback element is `PCM,1`, the chat mapping binds an element that is not there. `element_probe()` leaves `volume_use` at `IGNORE`, the path loads without a hardware volume, and the chat sink gets software volume, which is per-node and behaves fine. Nobody notices.

The Maxwell has two playback elements, one per USB Feature Unit:

| Function | Interface | Feature Unit | ALSA element | PCM |
|----------|-----------|--------------|--------------|-----|
| Chat | 1, `Chat-Audeze Maxwell` | 2 | `PCM,0` | `hw:%f,0,0` |
| Game |

+# Protocol support documentation
+
+Each protocol directory may contain a `support.xml` file documenting the
+support status of the protocol among member projects. These files are
+validated against `support.dtd` and must conform to the format described
+below.
+
+## Governance
+
+Member projects are free to add or update their own entries and notes at
+any time. Changes to a project's own support entries do not require
+review or approval beyond the normal merge request process. There are no
+additional merge requirements for support file changes.
+
+## Format
+
+A `support.xml` file has a root `<support>` element with a required
+`protocol` attribute identifying the protocol by name.
+
+Each member project is represented by a `<project>` element with a
+`name` attribute. A project contains one or more `<status>` elements
+and zero or more `<component>` elements.
+
+### Status
+
+The `<status>` element has a required `value` attribute and a required
+`protocol-version` attribute. `protocol-version` refers to the interface
+version of the protocol and means "up to and including this version."
+Multiple `<status>` elements may be used when a project's stance differs
+across protocol versions.
+
+The `value` attribute must be one of:
+
+- `supported` - The project implements the protocol.
+- `open` - The project is open to implementing the protocol but does
+  not yet support it. This covers the range from "actively working on
+  it" to "would accept a contribution." Use notes to clarify.
+- `unsupported` - The project does not support the protocol. This
+  covers both cases where the functionality is provided by a different
+  mechanism and where the project has decided against implementing it.
+  Use notes to explain the reasoning.
+
+An optional `<notes>` child element may provide additional context, such
+as the reason for the status or what alternative mechanism is used.
+
+### Component
+
+The `<component>` element documents support within a specific component
+of a member project (e.g. "mutter" and "gtk" within the "GNOME"
+project). Components should only be listed when they implement the
+protocol.
+
+Required attributes:
+
+- `name` - The name of the component.
+- `version` - The component version that introduced support.
+- `protocol-version` - The interface version of the protocol supported, up
+

title: Resend page context on Duo Chat retry
description:
## What does this MR do and why?

Duo Agentic Chat lets a user retry an assistant response. On the backend a retry forks the conversation from the checkpoint before the message being retried, so the discarded attempt never reaches the model.

The frontend decides separately which additional context to attach to each message it sends: the current page's URL and title, and the project's `AGENTS.md` or `chat-rules.md`. To avoid paying for the same context twice, it looks back through the conversation to see what it already sent. That look-back walks the flat local message list, which still contains every superseded retry attempt, and the result is cached until the browser page path changes.

Two things go wrong as a result. Retrying from a page whose context was only ever sent by the attempt being discarded sends no context at all, even though the forked conversation never received it. And after a retry, later messages compare themselves against the discarded attempt rather than against the conversation that actually survived.

This MR records the message ids that a fork leaves behind, derives the look-back from the filtered list the resumed run replays, and forces a recompute when the send is a retry so a same-page retry does not inherit the discarded attempt's bookkeeping. The messages themselves stay in the list, so a user can still browse previous attempts. The tracking is cleared when the thread is reset or reloaded, because a reloaded thread only contains the surviving conversation.

Expected behaviour, with "Say 3" and "Say 4" both retries of "Say 2":

```
Say 1 on page A          -> page A context is sent
Say 2 on page B          -> page B context is sent
Say 3 on page B (retry)  -> page B context is sent again; the forked
                            conversation never saw page B
Say 4 on page A (retry)  -> nothing is sent; page A went out with Say 1
```

title: backends/monitor: Offer perfect fractional scales up to denominator 5
description:
Since the exact-quotient rework (6791f4f8), mutter only advertises scales n/d that divide the mode resolution perfectly, searching denominators up to `MAX_DENOMINATOR` (4). That cap excludes perfectly valid scales and can leave large gaps between the offered options.

**Real-world case:** Apple MacBook Air M2 under Asahi Linux with the full 2560×1664 panel enabled (`appledrm show_notch=1`) offers only 100%, 133.33%, 200%, 266.67% — nothing between 133% and 200%. Yet 8/5 (160%, logical 1600×1040) divides the mode *exactly*; it is excluded only because its denominator is 5. Users of that panel are pushed from a comfortable 166.67% (valid at the cropped 2560×1600) to a choice between "too small" and "too big".

**What this MR does**

- Raises the denominator cap for the *offered* scales (and for scales accepted from stored configurations) from 4 to **5**. This admits only additional perfect scales — the exactness invariant is untouched — namely the 1/5 steps 120/140/160/180/240/320/360% where they divide the mode. Going higher was evaluated and rejected: 8 roughly doubles the list on common modes with awkward entries such as 114.29% and 171.43%; 5 is the sweet spot.
- **Keeps automatic default selection unchanged** via a separate `MAX_DEFAULT_DENOMINATOR` (4). Without this, e.g. a 1920×1080 14.5" panel would move from a 100% to a 120% default (the DPI heuristic legitimately prefers it) — that's a policy decision worth making explicitly, not as a side effect of offering more choices. Happy to drop the split if maintainers prefer defaults to consider the new scales too.

| Mode | Offered today (%) | Added (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 2560×1664 (MacBook Air 13.6) | 100, 133.33, 200, 266.67 | **160**, 320 |
| 2880×1864 (MacBook Air 15.3) | 100, 133.33, 200, 266.67 | **160** |
| 1920×1080 | 100, 125, 133.33, 150, 166.67, 200 | **120, 160** |
| 2560×1440 | 100, 125, 133.33, 166.67, 200, 250, 266.67 | **160**, 320 |
| 3840×2160 | 12 options | 120, 160, 240, 320 |

**Tests:** support

title: Draft: Migrate foundational flow lookups to named accessors

## What does this MR do and why?

The Duo Agent Platform accesses foundational flows by reference string (e.g., `code_review/v1`). 

Hardcoded string lookups are error-prone: typos return nil silently instead of failing immediately. !251999+ introduced named accessors like `FoundationalFlow.code_review_v1` to prevent this.

This MR completes that migration by replacing remaining string-based lookups with named accessors across the codebase The result is safer and clearer: typos fail fast with `NoMethodError`, and reference strings are not repeated across the codebase.

## References

Follow-up cleanup on !251999.

## How to set up and validate locally

Start a Code Review or Developer foundational flow from the UI (for example, mention `@duo` on a merge request) and confirm it starts and behaves the same as before - these flows now resolve through the named accessors under the hood.

## MR acceptance checklist

Evaluate this MR against the [MR acceptance checklist](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/code_review/#acceptance-checklist).
It helps you analyze changes to reduce risks in quality, performance, reliability, security, and maintainability.

title: UpdateItems regenerates pin KIIDs
description:
### Context

This patch is part of a series that came out of building **KICAD_MCP**, an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that lets
LLM agents drive a live KiCad session through KiCad's official IPC API — the
protobuf-over-socket interface that also backs `kicad-python`/`kipy`. The
agent does what a plugin would do, only continuously and headlessly: place
symbols and footprints, wire up hierarchical sheets, run ERC, update the PCB
from the schematic — all as `CreateItems` / `GetItems` / `UpdateItems` /
`SaveDocument` / … protobuf requests.

Driving the API at that intensity exercises paths no interactive session
hits: documents that are open but not displayed, sheets other than the active
one, both editors open against the same project, round-trips through the
clipboard S-expression format, and error paths that must come back as
protobuf statuses rather than dialogs (an IPC client cannot click "OK", so
any modal dialog reached from a handler hangs the client). A typical session
that surfaced several of the bugs in this series at once:

> create a sub-sheet → place a resistor on it while the root sheet is
> displayed → save all → run ERC from `kicad-cli` — each step crossed a
> different bug fixed below.

The branches are cut against `master` and are independent of each other
unless the section says otherwise.

### Authorship

The code was co-authored and reviewed with LLM assistance (**Claude-Fable-5** and **GLM**-5.1), under human direction, code-revision, and validated by
a human against a live KiCad build. Every branch compiles clean (Release,
`-DKICAD_BUILD_QA_TESTS=ON`) and went through two adversarial review rounds
before submission.

---

**Function:** symbol update path in
`API_HANDLER_SCH::handleCreateUpdateItemsInternal`, with the preservation
logic in `SCH_SYMBOL` (`eeschema/sch_symbol.cpp`).

**Expected:** updating a placed symbol over IPC (moving it, changing a
field) keeps the identity of its pins: anything that references a pin by
KIID — ERC markers

title: Fix missing interpolation options in Default Keyframe Type menu

Furthermore, `AssetParameterModel::getDefaultKeyframes()` contained hardcoded fallback logic that defaulted any selected keyframe type other than Discrete or Smooth to Linear (=). 

This MR populates the **Default Keyframe Type** menu dynamically in KeyframeContainer using `KeyframeModel::getKeyframeTypes()`, making all available interpolation types selectable as defaults. It also updates `AssetParameterModel::getDefaultKeyframes()` to retrieve separators via `KeyframeModel::getSeparatorForKeyframeType()`, ensuring newly created default keyframes are correctly serialized into parameter strings with the selected interpolation type.

title: gst: clamp a fraction that does not fit a GstFraction
description:
A SPA fraction is a pair of `uint32`; a `GstFraction` is a pair of `gint`. `handle_fraction_prop()` passes the values on unchecked, so a denominator above `INT32_MAX` arrives as a negative number and `gst_caps_set_simple()` refuses the range:

```
gst_value_collect_fraction_range: assertion 'gst_util_fraction_compare (...) < 0' failed
range start is not smaller than end for `GstFractionRange'
```

The whole `framerate` field is then missing from the caps.

### Where it comes from

A V4L2 source that reports a long maximum frame interval inverts into a small framerate whose denominator is that interval's numerator. Two drivers use `UINT32_MAX` there:

* `v4l2loopback`, with no producer attached — `V4L2LOOPBACK_FRAME_INTERVAL_MAX`;
* **`drivers/media/pci/mgb4/mgb4_vin.c`**, an in-tree capture driver, where `0xFFFFFFFF / MGB4_HW_FREQ` is an unremarkable slowest frame of **34 seconds**. The value is not silly; it is the denominator of the resulting framerate that does not fit.

### Measured

`v4l2loopback` advertising `Continuous 0.001s - 4294967295.000s`, arms interleaved:

```
                     GStreamer CRITICALs   framerate in the device caps
  master                     77                     absent
  with this patch             0             [ 1/2147483647, 1000/1 ]
  master again               77                     absent
```

The device's first caps structure on master, in full — there is no `framerate` in it:

```
video/x-raw, drm-format=(string)XR24, format=(string)DMA_DRM,
interlace-mode=(string)progressive, width=(int)[ 2, 8192 ],
height=(int)[ 1, 8192 ], colorimetry=(string)1:4:7:1;
```

A `facetimehd` camera enumerated in the same run has `framerate=(fraction)30/1`, so the field is not missing for some unrelated reason.

Reduce first, which is exact and enough for `mgb4` — gcd is 5, so `125000000/4294967295` becomes `25000000/858993459` — and scale only when that still does not fit, which is `v4l2loopback`'s irreducible `1/UINT32_MAX`.

### Overlap wit

title: docs: document running NetworkManager in a non-dracut initrd
description:
## Summary

Documents how to run NetworkManager in an initrd that is not dracut's.

## Purpose

The initrd units were decoupled from dracut in 1.54, in commit 8640ea822f, explicitly "allowing other systemd-based initrd generators to take advantage of it". No documentation followed. The result is that the feature exists, ships on distributions that do not strip it, and is undiscoverable.

This came out of a user question on IRC: they had found the units, could not find any documentation for them, and asked how to use them to bring up networking early enough to unlock an encrypted root over SSH.

Please read https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/NetworkManager/NetworkManager/-/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md before opening the merge request. In particular, check that:

- [x] The subject for all commits is concise, explanatory, and includes a prefix indicating the area of code changed (e.g., "nmcli: ", "core: ")
- [x] The message for all commits explains the reason for the change

title: array: Handle GArrays adding their own elements
description:
This problem came up internally at RH while we were discussing side effects of an AI report: Do we need to handle `g_array_append/prepend/insert_vals()` with `data` pointing into the array?  
Because that would be bad as `g_array_maybe_expand()` can happen and call `g_realloc()` the array and then the data pointer points into invalid memory.

Initially that sounded preposterous, because who would do that?

But the longer we thought about it, the more likely it became. Not deliberately, but it isn't hard to imagine that some API returns an element of an array as a const pointer somewhere. And then some code wants to add it to some list where it potentially doesn't even know that it is actually an element of that list and then some code ends up via some indirections adding its own elements to an array.

So now that we considered it a serious problem - especially because in the example above nobody would even understand that it could happen or why, which would make it potentially nasty security issue - can we do something about it.  
And that's where the first commit came from: We can add `g_array_contains_pointer()` and just `return_if_fail()` if that happens. That at least avoids security problems.

But then, it turned out that this might be overeager. C++ `std::vector` explicitly allows `push_back()` if the vector does not reallocate, ie it allows applications to call `vector::resize(); vector::push_back();` to append elements of itself. Our commit had just forbidden that.

That's when we had the idea that we can split the code of `g_array_append_vals()` into 2 paths: the normal path and the self-append path where we turn the data pointer into an offset that stays valid after a realloc. So I implemented that.

And after I had implemented that, I realized that the same approach would work for `g_array_prepend_vals()` and `g_array_insert_vals()`, too. So I implemented it there, too.

And that's this MR, which now makes it valid to call these functions with elements po

title: Draft: magnifier: Map touchscreen input to zoomed content
description:
The screen magnifier displays transformed clones of the desktop, but touchscreen events continue to use untransformed stage coordinates. Consequently, a touch can be delivered to a different actor or surface than the one shown under the user's finger.

Publish the viewport-to-source mappings for active zoom regions to Mutter. Mutter can then transform absolute input coordinates before Clutter performs actor picking.

Mappings are kept synchronized when zoom regions are enabled, disabled, resized or animated. Updates are coalesced and applied before the next redraw so that Mutter receives the geometry corresponding to the displayed magnifier state.

Use the introspectable `Meta.MagnifierInputMapping` record rather than positional arrays. The named fields make the coordinate-space contract explicit and leave the interface reusable by other absolute input devices, such as styluses.

This depends on the corresponding Mutter MR and must be merged after it:

Mutter MR: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/mutter/-/merge_requests/5284

### Testing

- Added unit coverage for inverse coordinate transforms, invalid input and mapping equality.
- Verified the changes with ESLint.
- Built the paired GNOME Shell and Mutter changes successfully.
- Manually tested touchscreen interaction in full-screen and docked magnifier modes.
author: Kacper
diff:
--- js/misc/magnifierUtils.js
+++ js/misc/magnifierUtils.js
@@ -0,0 +1,76 @@
+// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Kacper Laska
+// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
+
+/**
+ * @typedef {object} InputMapping
+ * @property {number} viewportX
+ * @property {number} viewportY
+ * @property {number} viewportWidth
+ * @property {number} viewportHeight
+ * @property {number} sourceOriginX
+ * @property {number} sourceOriginY
+ * @property {number} sourceScaleX
+ * @property {number} sourceScaleY
+ */
+
+/**
+ * createInputMapping:
+ *
+ * Build an inverse mapping from an on-stage magnifier viewport and the
+ * current transform of the desktop clone inside that viewport.
+ *
+ * @param {{x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number}} viewport
+ * @param {{x: number, y: number, scaleX: number, scaleY: number}} clone
+ * @returns {InputMapping | null} the inverse input mapping
+ */
+export function createInputMapping(viewport, clone) {
+    const inputValues = [
+        viewport.x,
+        viewport.y,
+        viewport.width,
+        viewport.height,
+        clone.x,
+        clone.y,
+        clone.scaleX,
+        clone.scaleY,
+    ];
+
+    if (!inputValues.every(Number.isFinite) ||
+        viewport.width <= 0 || viewport.height <= 0 ||
+        clone.scaleX <= 0 || clone.scaleY <= 0)
+        return null;
+
+    const mapping = {
+        viewportX: viewport.x,
+        viewportY: viewport.y,
+        viewportWidth: viewport.width,
+        viewportHeight: viewport.height,
+        sourceOriginX: -clone.x / clone.scaleX,
+        sourceOriginY: -clone.y / clone.scaleY,
+        sourceScaleX: 1 / clone.scaleX,
+        sourceScaleY: 1 / clone.scaleY,
+    };
+
+    if (!Object.values(mapping).every(Number.isFinite) ||
+        !Number.isFinite(viewport.x + viewport.width) ||
+        !Number.isFinite(viewport.y + viewport.height))
+        return null;
+
+    return mapping;
+}
+
+/**
+ * @param {InputMapping} first
+ * @param {InputMapping} second
+ * @returns {boolean} whether both mappings have identical values
+ */
+export function inputMappingEqual(first, second) {
+    return first.viewportX === second.viewportX &&
+        first.viewportY === second.viewportY &&
+        first.viewportWidth === second.viewportWidth &&
+        first.viewportHeight === second.viewportHeight &&
+        first.sourceOriginX === second.sourceOriginX &&
+        first.sourceOriginY === second.sourceOriginY &&
+        first.sourceScaleX === second.sourceScaleX &&
+        first.sourceScaleY === second.sourceScaleY;
+}

title: gstpipewiresrc: copy the last free buffer instead of stalling the stream
description:
Closes #5363.

A buffer goes back to the producer as soon as it has been passed on, so a consumer holding the whole
pool leaves the producer with nothing to fill and the stream stops rather than degrading. With the
four buffers a v4l2 source negotiates, a consumer holding four is enough.

Handing over the last free buffer is the moment that decides it, and the last moment that buffer can
still be made to come back. So copy it there instead of sharing it: the pool buffer returns
immediately and the element degrades into a memcpy instead of stopping.

This is the shape that was asked for here twice:

> How about stating to copy the buffers when the gstreamer source is lagging for more than X
> buffers? — @wtaymans, !1917

> We recently discussed wanted to automatically start copying if we are running out of buffers, but
> this has not been implemented yet. — @arun, #4797

## When it engages, and what that costs

There is no threshold to pick. The test is `n_outstanding + 1 >= n_buffers` — this dequeue is taking
the last free buffer — and it is relative to the pool that was actually negotiated. Not a property,
following @ocrete's point in !1917 that it should come from what PipeWire allocated rather than from
something the application sets.

**The cost is not zero before it is needed, and that is worth being explicit about.** The decision
has to be taken *before* the buffer is handed over, from how many are outstanding at that instant.
That number cannot tell a consumer that returns the buffer at once from one that keeps it — both
look identical at that moment. The smaller the pool, the less room there is between the two.

Measured on a MacBookPro14,1 (facetimehd) and on a Lenovo with a UVC camera, appsink holding N
samples referenced, pool size set with `max-buffers`, arms alternated run by run, and every frame
classified as shared or copied by two independent signals that had to agree (`GstMemory.parent`, and
whether `GstParentBufferMeta` is present):

| pool | held

These merge request controllers read request params directly, bypassing Rails StrongParameters. They were flagged by `Rails/StrongParams` and listed in `.rubocop_todo/rails/strong_params.yml`.

title: nvk: Track shader-backed transfer writes for barriers
description:
### What does this MR do and why?

<!--Describe in detail what your merge request does and why.-->

```
Some COPY-stage transfer writes in NVK are implemented using compute
meta, so a subsequent transfer-write dependency needs to flush shader
data. Other transfer operations use graphics or copy engines and don't
dirty shader data.

Track whether shader-backed transfer state is unknown, clean, or dirty
within a command buffer:

- command buffers start UNKNOWN, preserving the existing conservative
  behavior across command-buffer boundaries
- an actual shader-data flush transitions the state to CLEAN
- compute-meta transfer writes transition it to DIRTY
- COPY-stage transfer-write flushes can be skipped while the state is
  known CLEAN
- secondary command-buffer state is propagated conservatively
- CmdCopyQueryPoolResults is tracked because NVK implements it using a
  compute shader

This avoids redundant shader-data flushes without assuming state across
independently recorded command buffers.

### Performance

GTA V Enhanced, VKD3D-Proton, descriptor-buffer path, RTX 3090 / GA102:

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Average FPS | 71.785 | 72.989 | +1.678% |
| 1% low | 54.398 | 56.648 | +4.137% |
| 0.1% low | 47.522 | 48.479 | +2.014% |
| Long pass FPS | 71.862 | 73.208 | +1.873% |

### Testing

Mesa unit tests:

- 30 passed
- 0 failed
- Nouveau/NVK `nil`, `nak`, `mme_builder`, and `nvk_mme` passed

Targeted Vulkan CTS, VK-GL-CTS
0b04c470ed78569b0b778ece1262d88455ab2b00:

- 139 selected cases
- 66 passed
- 73 not supported
- 0 failed
- 0 warnings

Executed coverage included:

- copy/fill: 33 passed
- query-copy: 15 passed
- synchronization: 21 passed
- events: 13 passed
- secondary command buffers: 7 passed
```

title: Prefix REST reference deep links with the document slug
description:
> [!WARNING]
> Merge this MR only once Artifact Registry's is ready to be published

## What does this MR do and why?

The interactive REST reference at https://api.gitlab.com/rest/ is gaining a second OpenAPI document. Scalar keeps the document slug out of URL fragments while only one document is configured, and puts it into every fragment as soon as there are two. So `#tag/offline-transfers` stops resolving and `#gitlab/tag/offline-transfers` starts.

Both directions fail silently. The fragment is left as typed, nothing is logged, and the reader lands at the top of the correct document with no sign that an anchor was meant to apply. This updates the four deep links under `doc/` so they keep working.

The switch is atomic — no build accepts both shapes — so these links cannot be made correct for both, and this MR has to land immediately after the reference starts rendering two documents rather than before. Until then, the links here point at a fragment production does not yet resolve.

Fragment links in issue and MR comments are out of scope: they are discussion artifacts rather than a maintained surface. Personal bookmarks will break and cannot be found from the repository.

## References

Related to: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/608507

Part of: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/quality/-/epics/428

## Screenshots or screen recordings

## How to set up and validate locally

Fragments are resolved client-side and never reach the server, so `curl` cannot check this; it needs a browser against a build that renders two documents.

Measured with Playwright against such a build, asserting `window.scrollY` on a fresh page per URL:

```
#gitlab/tag/offline-transfers                              scrolls
#gitlab/tag/offline-transfers/POST/api/v4/offline_exports  scrolls
#tag/offline-transfers/POST/api/v4/offline_exports         does not scroll
```

A fresh page per URL matters: two URLs differing only in the fragment make a same-document navigation,

title: kitemviews: take the room for the values of an item at once
description:
The values of an item are inserted one role at a time, and the vector behind them grows into each pair
as it arrives: for the five roles of a details view it ends up with room for eight, having left the
room for one, two and four behind it.

Every role of the view is a pair the item is about to hold, give or take the few that only some items
have, so the room is taken once before the roles are inserted. For 100000 items of five roles that is
336 bytes an item rather than 512.
author: meven

title: backends/drm: don't access pipelines in the commit thread
description:
All pending state of pipelines may be modified at any time by the main thread,
including the crtc.
To fix that, this more explicitly tracks which crtc a pageflip event should be
delivered for.

Fixes a regression caused by !9518. When that MR is backported to 6.7, this must be included as well.

description:

## Change description

This implements feature-request: https://gitlab.com/kicad/code/kicad/-/work_items/25337

With this change, PCBs designed in Allegro 25.1 can be imported in kicad. A few tweaks were done to the header decoder to make it work.

Claude AI Opus 4.8 assisted getting to the bottom of how a few details in the header changed - by being told to try to read a 25.1 file based on what kicad already knows about .brd files.

Tested with a real design originally made in 25.1. Also test imported an older design made in 23.1 and 24.1 to ensure no regression.
